findings: The official monthly series records a 12 per cent reduction in regional road deaths between the year to May 2022 and the year to November 2025, not 40 per cent. No published series supports a 40 per cent figure over any comparable period.
context: The comparison uses 12-month rolling totals to remove seasonal effects. Individual months vary widely. An updated release in September 2026 puts the reduction at 13 per cent; the classification is unchanged.

findings: The national accounts show real household disposable income per capita fell 4.6 per cent between the June quarter 2022 and the December quarter 2025. Nominal household disposable income rose 11 per cent over the same period. Neither series shows an 8 per cent fall.
context: 'Household disposable income' can be measured in nominal or real terms, in aggregate or per person. The per-capita real measure fell; the aggregate nominal measure rose. Mr Oyelaran subsequently corrected the figure to 'around 5 per cent in real per-capita terms'.

findings: This is a general evaluative statement. Whether Australians are 'worse off' depends on the measure chosen (real wages, disposable income, wealth, wellbeing surveys) and the comparison period. PUBLIC RECORD logs the statement for context and does not assess it.
context: Where a politician attaches a specific figure to a statement like this, the figure is recorded and checked as a separate claim.

findings: Program reporting records 40,300 dwellings approved for funding by 31 March 2026, of which 17,900 were completed. The 40,000 figure is accurate for approvals but not for completed homes.
context: 'Delivered' is ambiguous. Program documents distinguish approvals, commencements and completions. On 6 May 2026 Senator Natarajan restated the figure as 40,000 approved and around 18,000 complete.

findings: The market operator's quarterly report shows the volume-weighted average spot price for the March quarter 2026 was 18.4 per cent higher than in the March quarter 2025.
context: Wholesale prices are one component of retail bills; the claim was specifically about wholesale prices.

findings: The only published analysis is a cost-benefit summary commissioned by the port's proponent, which reports a benefit-cost ratio of 3.1 but does not publish its assumptions. No independent evaluation has been located.
context: A single proponent-commissioned source is below the evidence standard for a contested economic claim. The record will be updated if an independent evaluation is published.

findings: Departmental program data lists 1,940 kilometres of funded regional road upgrades, of which 1,120 kilometres were complete at February 2026. The figure is close for funded works; completed works are lower.
context: The claim referred to funded upgrades, which the data broadly supports. It would be contradicted if read as completed works.

findings: The initial June quarter 2026 rental price index showed annual growth of 5.1 per cent, higher than the 4.8 per cent recorded in 2021. On that release, the past year was not the slowest since 2020.
context: Superseded on 12 September 2026 after the series was revised.

findings: The September 2026 revision of the rental price index revised June quarter annual growth to 4.6 per cent nationally, below 2021. On the revised series the claim holds for the capital-city index (4.4 per cent) but not for the regional index (5.3 per cent).
context: Classification changed from 'Contradicted by evidence' to 'Mixed / context required' after revised data became available. The earlier assessment remains on the record.

findings: The statement describes a private conversation. The regulator has said it does not comment on private discussions. No record exists against which the claim can be tested.
context: Unverifiable claims are recorded so that later evidence can be attached, but they are not counted as supported or contradicted.

findings: This repeats a claim first checked on 9 January 2026. The updated August 2026 release of the official series records a 13 per cent reduction in regional road deaths over the comparable period, not 40 per cent.
context: The evidence was refreshed with the August 2026 release before this repetition was assessed. The result is unchanged.

findings: Taxation statistics for 2023–24 show Tasmania recorded the lowest median taxable income of any state or territory.
context: Median taxable income excludes people who do not lodge returns and is not the same as median household income.

findings: The national inventory records that emissions fell 1.2 per cent in 2023 and 0.8 per cent in 2024, and rose 0.4 per cent in 2025. Emissions did not rise in every year since 2022.
context: Annual inventory figures are revised over time. The claim was repeated unchanged on 12 August 2026.

findings: This is a prediction about future growth. It cannot be assessed against current evidence. It is logged so that it can be revisited if relevant data becomes available.

Net overseas migration peaked at 536,000 in 2022–23. The latest annual figure, 335,000 in 2024–25, is below that peak but well above the pre-2020 average. The cumulative three-year total is the highest on record.
context: 'Record levels' is accurate for the three-year cumulative total and inaccurate for the latest annual figure. Mr Oyelaran clarified on 29 September 2026 that he was referring to the cumulative total.

findings: Departmental Medicare statistics record a GP bulk-billing rate of 79.0 per cent for the June quarter 2026.
context: The bulk-billing rate counts services, not patients; the share of patients who are always bulk-billed is lower.

findings: The 2025 national assessment report puts 33.1 per cent of Tasmanian Year 9 students in the two lowest reading proficiency bands ('needs additional support' and 'developing'). Only 12.4 per cent are in the lowest band. The figure matches one reading of the data but not another, and applies to Year 9 rather than all students.
context: The assessment program replaced the old 'national minimum standard' with proficiency bands in 2023, so there is no longer a single 'minimum standard' figure.

findings: Budget Paper No. 1 for 2026–27 projects defence funding at 2.3 per cent of GDP in 2028–29.
context: Projections depend on GDP forecasts and are revised at each budget update.

findings: State recorded-crime statistics show burglary offences in the Wattle Plains local area rose 23 per cent over the two years to June 2026. They did not double.
context: Mr Oyelaran clarified on 3 August 2026 that he 'should have said break-ins have risen sharply, not doubled'.

findings: The latest published hospital resources data covers 2024–25 and shows Silvergum Hospital with 412 beds, 64 fewer than in 2020–21. No published data covers 2025–26, so the claimed 200-bed reduction cannot be tested for the full period.
context: PUBLIC RECORD has requested current bed numbers from the hospital network. The record will be updated when a response is received.

findings: Stockholm International Peace Research Institute data for 2023 record Australian military spending of US$32.3 billion against Taiwan's US$16.6 billion, roughly double. Australia's nominal GDP (about US$1.87 trillion) is, however, more than twice Taiwan's (about US$802 billion), so Taiwan spends more as a share of its economy (2.2 per cent against 1.9 per cent). The 'similar size economy' comparison holds only on a purchasing-power-parity basis (CIA World Factbook: Taiwan US$1.14 trillion in 2019, Australia US$1.33 trillion in 2022), which three experts told AAP FactCheck was a problematic basis for comparing military spending because hardware is bought in US dollars and Taiwan relies on conscription. On a consistent purchasing-power basis the Lowy Institute put 2022 spending at US$36.9 billion for Australia and US$30 billion for Taiwan.
context: AAP FactCheck rated other figures in the same video accurate, including that Australia's per-capita military spending had roughly doubled since 2003 and was about three times Japan's and six times China's. A representative for Senator Shoebridge pointed AAP FactCheck to CIA World Factbook purchasing-power-parity GDP figures as the basis for the economic comparison. AAP FactCheck's 'Mixture' rating means the claim includes accurate information but also significant errors or problems.

findings: The bill would allow the immigration minister to designate any country a 'removal concern country' if the minister thought it in the national interest, after which that country's citizens outside Australia could not make valid visa applications, with exemptions for dual nationals, the partners, children and parents of Australians, and refugee and humanitarian applicants. The explanatory memorandum describes the designation as a 'discretionary personal power'. Legal experts from the Kaldor Centre, the University of Sydney, the University of Technology Sydney and the University of Queensland, and the Law Council of Australia, told RMIT ABC Fact Check that the discretion was exceptionally broad with very limited scope for judicial review, and broader than the United States visa-sanction power that the Trump administration applied to nine countries between 2017 and 2020, which mostly targeted government officials. One expert noted that a court could strike down an unreasonable designation, so 'literally any country' is not certain in practice.
context: RMIT ABC Fact Check found the claim 'a fair call'. The bill was introduced after the High Court's NZYQ decision ended indefinite immigration detention; the government described the power as a diplomatic tool to encourage countries to accept the return of their nationals. A spokesman for Senator Shoebridge told Fact Check that while there were 'some minor differences' from the Trump-era orders, 'the purpose of the bill is the same'.

findings: Defence officials told Senate estimates on 25 October 2023 that 351 export permits relating to Israel had been issued since 1 January 2017, but that permits cover 'military and dual-use' goods such as radios, sporting equipment and vehicle parts, and that none of the 322 permits issued between January 2017 and 31 March 2023 was for 'lethal equipment'. ABS trade data showed exports to Israel in the 'arms and ammunition' category averaging about $2.6 million a year over the five years to 2022 and $8,000 in the first nine months of 2023; Australia's Arms Trade Treaty reports record six 'small arms and light weapons' sent in 2016 and 2017. Defence Minister Richard Marles said on 7 November 2023 that 'Israel has not sought any weapons from Australia and we have not provided any'. Defence analysts told Fact Check the export data are opaque, and an editor's note added on 13 December 2023 said the available data may not capture inputs to international supply chains, such as components for weapons systems.
context: RMIT ABC Fact Check published this analysis in its CheckMate newsletter without a verdict label. PUBLIC RECORD classifies the claim as mixed: the available official data do not show sales of complete weapons to Israel in the period, while the permit system covers a broad range of military and dual-use goods and the data do not capture components supplied through international supply chains. No direct response from Senator Shoebridge to the fact-check is recorded; the Greens subsequently tabled a petition calling for an end to military exports to Israel.

findings: Funding data supplied to AAP FactCheck by Foodbank Australia showed its total federal funding fell from $1.4 million in 2013-14 to $1.3 million in 2014-15, $1.05 million in 2015-16 and $750,000 a year from 2016-17 to 2018-19, before rising to $16.2 million in 2019-20 during the pandemic. That was a reduction, but far smaller than $20 million a year. Department of Social Services financial statements show that spending on the broader financial wellbeing and capability program, which funds Foodbank among other hardship charities, fell by about $25 million a year between 2014-15 ($124.94 million) and 2017-18 ($99.97 million), which AAP FactCheck said supported the Treasurer's broader statement about 'these programs' but not the Foodbank-specific figure.
context: The Prime Minister first referred to the Foodbank cut on 5 November 2025, citing the Treasurer, who had told the House that day that the Coalition 'cut $20 million a year from these programs'. The Prime Minister's office did not respond to AAP FactCheck's request for evidence.

findings: Voting records and shadow-minister statements show the Coalition supported several of the government's measures: it matched the $8.5 billion Medicare bulk-billing commitment dollar for dollar in February 2025, spoke and voted for the legislation cutting the PBS co-payment in September 2025, supported the $573 million women's health package, announced a matching freeze on draught beer excise in March 2025, and supported the 2024 extension of paid parental leave to 26 weeks while proposing amendments. The Coalition did oppose other measures, including the student debt cut, free TAFE, the Housing Australia Future Fund and build-to-rent tax changes.
context: AAP FactCheck noted that in the same answer the Prime Minister repeated the claim that the Coalition had opposed every round of energy bill relief, which it had earlier found to be wrong, and that the increase in the superannuation guarantee to 12 per cent for which he claimed credit was legislated in 2011. The Prime Minister's office did not respond to a request for evidence.

findings: Parliamentary records show the Coalition voted against the December 2022 legislation that created the Energy Bill Relief Fund and funded the first round, although the then Opposition Leader said it would have supported the subsidies if they had been separated from the coal and gas price caps in the same bill. The $300 extension in the 2024-25 budget passed in an appropriation bill without Coalition opposition after the Opposition Leader confirmed support in his budget reply of 17 May 2024. The third round, announced in the 2025-26 budget, lapsed at the dissolution of Parliament, was reintroduced in July 2025, and the then Shadow Treasurer had said in March 2025 the Coalition would not oppose it. AAP FactCheck found no evidence the Coalition opposed the second or third rounds.
context: The Prime Minister made a similar statement during the 2025 election campaign ('We provided that $300, then another $300, both of which were opposed by the Coalition') and repeated the claim in Question Time on 3 November 2025, after the fact-check was published. The Prime Minister's office did not respond to AAP FactCheck's request for evidence.

findings: The figure traces to a 2014-15 Treasury estimate, given in answer to a Senate estimates question, that replacing Labor's school funding indexation with indexation to inflation plus enrolment growth would reduce projected Commonwealth spending by about $28 billion between 2017-18 and 2024-25. That was a reduction in the projected rate of future increases, not a cut to existing funding. The 2014 budget committed to the four funded years of Labor's 2013 plan; Labor's six-year plan had only about a third of its cost budgeted and four jurisdictions signed up. Public finance experts consulted by AAP FactCheck described the change as a re-estimation of unfunded commitments rather than a cut.
context: The Labor campaign referred AAP FactCheck to page seven of the 2014 budget overview as evidence. The Prime Minister made the claim several times during the 2025 campaign, including in both the Sky News and ABC leaders' debates; the Education Minister used the same figure. The dispute is over whether a reduction in projected future growth should be described as money 'ripped out'.

findings: The figure originated in analysis by the Treasurer's office, which combined ABS average weekly earnings, the 2024 tax cuts and energy bill relief, without adjusting for inflation, and assumed that average earnings growth over the Coalition's 2013-2022 term would simply have continued. Economists consulted by AAP FactCheck said real wages, measured by the wage price index less inflation, fell for most of the government's term and had only recently turned positive; one inflation-adjusted calculation showed real earnings essentially unchanged under both governments. They also said the counterfactual ignored low unemployment and independent Fair Work Commission and Reserve Bank decisions.
context: The Treasurer first publicised the $7,200 figure in January 2025 and told AAP FactCheck that 'Australians are earning more and keeping more of what they earn under Labor, and they would be working much longer for less under Peter Dutton'. The Prime Minister repeated it in Question Time on 4 February 2025, as recorded here, and AAP FactCheck's later election-debate coverage noted he used it twice in the third leaders' debate. Other ministers repeated it on social media.

findings: ABS labour force data show there were 789,700 more employed people in February 2024 than in May 2022, the largest such increase for a first-term government since 1966, the earliest year for which broadly comparable data exist. Labour economists told RMIT ABC Fact Check that raw numbers ignore population growth: adjusted for population, the increase in employment during the first 21 months of the Hawke government in 1983-84 was larger, and that government also fared better on hours worked, underemployment and the share of new jobs that were full-time. Experts also said governments cannot take sole credit for job creation, most of which occurs in the private sector.
context: The Prime Minister and other senior ministers made similar statements from May 2023 onwards, including on X on 19 March 2024 and in an opinion piece in April 2024. The raw figure is accurate; the fact-check's qualifications concern the measure used and the attribution of credit.

findings: Former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull held bilateral meetings with Philippine presidents in the Philippines in November 2015 and November 2017, but on both occasions he was in the country for multilateral summits (APEC in 2015 and ASEAN in 2017). The Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet told AAP FactCheck it defines a bilateral visit as one 'not conducted in the margins of a regional or multilateral summit or conference'. On that definition the claim holds; one international relations expert said that in practical terms a meeting on the sidelines of a summit is 'the same thing'.
context: The claim also appeared in a media release from the Prime Minister's office on 11 August 2023 announcing the visit. AAP FactCheck rated it mostly true because it omits the context of Mr Turnbull's meetings.

findings: The National Indigenous Australians Agency told CheckMate that the Uluru Statement from the Heart is a one-page document, as confirmed by its authors. The 26-page document cited by critics was one of several documents released on the agency's freedom-of-information disclosure log in March 2023; it contains the one-page statement together with background material from the Referendum Council's regional dialogues, which the council's 2017 final report also reproduces.
context: The statement was made after a Sky News presenter and the Shadow Minister for Indigenous Australians said a 26-page version of the Uluru Statement had been 'exposed' through freedom of information. The dispute was part of the 2023 Voice referendum campaign. CheckMate did not use a one-word verdict label; its finding is quoted as the verdict.

findings: The Parliamentary Budget Office's 2025 Election Commitments Report found that the Coalition's policies would have increased deficits in 2025-26 and 2026-27 but reduced cumulative deficits by $6.6 billion over the four years to 2028-29, with net debt $49.9 billion and gross debt $81.7 billion lower over that period. Over the medium term, deficits were projected to be $162.4 billion larger between 2031-32 and 2035-36 and net debt $275.6 billion higher between 2033-34 and 2035-36, driven mainly by the Coalition's commitment to defence spending of 3 per cent of GDP and its 23.9 per cent tax-to-GDP cap. Budget experts consulted by AAP FactCheck said the claim was reasonable for the medium term but not for the forward estimates, and that decade-long projections are unreliable.
context: The Treasurer's office referred AAP FactCheck to the Parliamentary Budget Office report and to the Coalition's own costings, and said the costings did not fully capture the potential cost of the Coalition's nuclear policy. Other ministers made similar statements in February 2026. AAP FactCheck's 'Mixture' rating means the claim includes accurate information but also significant errors or problems.

findings: ABS monthly consumer price data show gas and other household fuels rose 34 per cent between May 2022 and February 2025, and quarterly data show insurance rose 35 per cent between June 2022 and December 2024. AAP FactCheck replicated the Coalition's electricity figure of about 32 per cent on the ABS index that excludes government rebates, although electricity prices including rebates rose only about 1 per cent. Food and non-alcoholic beverages rose 13 per cent, well below the 30 per cent grocery figure, which Mr Taylor's office sourced from an unpublished News Corp supermarket basket analysis. Three of the four figures the Treasurer said were made up were supported by official data on the measures the Coalition used.
context: The exchange occurred during the 2025 election campaign. The grocery figure was not supported by ABS data, but the gas, insurance and ex-rebate electricity figures were. The Treasurer's office did not respond to AAP FactCheck's request for evidence that the numbers were made up.

findings: The evidence the ministers' offices supplied to AAP FactCheck, an ABC Insiders interview with the Opposition Leader in February 2025, an interview with the Shadow Treasurer in May 2024 and the Opposition Leader's 2023 budget reply, shows the phrase 'wasteful spending' was used about federal public service numbers and the NDIS, not about indexation. The Shadow Treasurer's $45 billion figure for spending the Coalition had opposed excluded social security payments. AAP FactCheck found no record of the Opposition Leader describing indexation as wasteful, and the opposition confirmed that cutting indexation was not on its agenda. Social policy experts said the transcripts did not support the claim.
context: The release was issued during the lead-up to the 2025 election; the Minister for Social Services had made a similar claim a few days earlier. AAP FactCheck's verdict applied to the joint statement by both ministers.

findings: Figures supplied by Treasury and verified by RMIT ABC Fact Check against budget documents show the government returned 88.4 per cent of its tax revenue upgrades to the budget since taking office, while the Coalition returned 44.7 per cent over seven revenue upgrades. Using the Grattan Institute's broader method, which also counts lower-than-expected expenses and other variations, Fact Check calculated 85.4 per cent for Labor and 45.1 per cent for the Coalition. Experts noted the Coalition's figures span the pandemic, when banking windfalls was arguably not prudent, and that these figures alone do not settle which party is the better fiscal manager.
context: The Treasurer made the statement ahead of the May 2024 budget. The 'around 40 per cent' figure for the Coalition is slightly below the 44.7 per cent that Treasury's figures show.

findings: The Senate estimates recording of 26 February 2025 shows Senator Ruston was arguing that Labor's social media posts about its $8.5 billion plan to lift bulk billing to 90 per cent by 2030 were misleading because not every visit would be free. She said the Coalition had 'never said that Australians will get access to free GP services without exception', then confirmed the Coalition supported bulk billing and, asked whether she wanted Australians to have free access, replied 'No, I do want them to have free access'. The Coalition had committed to match the bulk-billing policy. Other quotes in the release, from Sussan Ley and Peter Dutton, concerned free TAFE and energy and university-debt subsidies rather than Medicare.
context: AAP FactCheck also found that a Labor Party social media video cut the words 'without exception' from Senator Ruston's remark. Mr Butler's office did not provide a response to AAP FactCheck's request for evidence. The release date is inferred from its reference to the estimates hearing that day.

findings: Department of Health Medicare statistics for GP non-referred attendances, the measure used in the minister's own release, show the bulk-billing rate rose from 83.1 per cent in the December quarter 2013 to 87 per cent in the June quarter 2022, peaking at 92.5 per cent in June 2020 during pandemic telehealth arrangements. The rate was declining from mid-2021 but fell much faster after the May 2022 election, to 76.5 per cent by the end of 2023; even after the two-point rise the minister cited following the November 2023 incentive increase, the March quarter 2024 rate was about ten points below its level at the election. Health economists told AAP FactCheck the rate was 'certainly declining' before the election but not in free fall, and that the decline was largely structural and would have occurred under either government.
context: Mr Butler's office confirmed the release's figures referred to GP non-referred attendances but, as the basis for 'free fall', pointed to a different measure, the share of adult concession card holders always bulk billed, which it said fell five percentage points in the four years to June 2022; it declined to provide comparable post-election figures for that measure. AAP FactCheck's 2025 election coverage recorded the Prime Minister using the 'free fall' description and referred back to this verdict.

findings: The $347 billion figure is the difference between total payments projected in the Coalition's 2022 Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Outlook and those in the government's 2024-25 Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook for 2023-24 to 2027-28; most of the gap reflects economic parameters such as inflation, which was 6.1 per cent when the government took office against the 4.25 per cent assumed in the outlook. The Opposition Leader cited the $347 billion as Labor overspending but did not describe it as the scope of any cuts, repeatedly ruled out cuts to Medicare and promised to match the government's $8.5 billion bulk-billing commitment. AAP FactCheck found that Labor's claim mischaracterised his comments, and separately that the Coalition's use of the figure left out key context.
context: Senator Gallagher's office directed AAP FactCheck to public statements by Coalition members about the $347 billion figure, including the Opposition Leader, as evidence. The Treasurer and other Labor figures used the same claim. AAP FactCheck did not assign a one-word verdict.

findings: NAB's 17 August 2026 economic newsletter described an illustrative scenario: if rental yields rose by one percentage point and property prices stayed flat, Sydney and Melbourne rents would need to rise by 25 to 30 per cent. It said any adjustment was more likely to combine lower dwelling prices and higher rents. In a note issued on 18 August, before the question was asked, NAB stated that the figure 'was not a forecast'. Ray White, whose modelling produced a similar figure, said its scenario assumed no price falls, which it considered unlikely, and was 'not a forecast of rent growth'. No published NAB material forecast a 30 per cent rise in rents.
context: The question concerned the changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax announced in the May 2026 budget. Mr Taylor's office told AAP FactCheck the claim was based on a section of NAB's newsletter as reported by The Australian, and on Ray White research. Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume made a similar claim the next day; it is recorded separately.

findings: Mr Taylor's office said the figure compared the ABS net overseas migration estimate for the year to September 2025 (311,000) with the forecast of 225,000 for 2026-27 in the December 2024 Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook, a gap of 86,000. The 2026-27 financial year had not begun. Compared with the forecast for the year in progress, 2025-26, of 260,000 in the December 2025 MYEFO, the overshoot was about 51,000. The May 2026 budget later raised the forecasts to 295,000 for 2025-26 and 245,000 for 2026-27. Experts consulted by AAP FactCheck said the like-for-like comparison was with the 2025-26 forecast, while noting that forecasts have routinely undershot actual migration since the pandemic under both governments.
context: Migration has exceeded the government's forecasts in several recent years; the dispute is over which forecast the latest actual figure should be compared with. Mr Taylor repeated the figure on ABC Insiders on 26 April 2026.

findings: A Parliamentary Library chronology shows that the Morrison government's Fuel Quality Standards (Petrol) Determination 2019 set a 10 parts-per-million sulphur limit from 1 July 2027, and that in 2021-22 the Coalition paid Ampol and Viva Energy $137.5 million each to meet the lower limit by the end of 2024 without legislating that date. The Albanese government legislated a 2024 deadline in 2022, then moved it to December 2025. Ampol told the ASX in October 2025 that its refinery upgrade would not be finished before mid-2026, and it exported higher-sulphur petrol in the meantime. After the standards were temporarily relaxed from 12 March 2026, Ampol said it could supply an extra 80 to 100 million litres a month domestically. The exports were connected to the compliance deadline the current government set, but the standard itself originated under the Coalition.
context: Mr Taylor's office pointed AAP FactCheck to the Parliamentary Library chronology and to the December 2023 announcement by Energy Minister Chris Bowen of stricter sulphur and aromatics limits from December 2025. Mr Taylor made a similar statement on 2GB radio on 16 March 2026 and in a Facebook reel.

findings: ABS private new capital expenditure grew by an average of about 1 per cent a quarter between the June quarter 2022 and the June quarter 2025, plateauing over the most recent 18 months rather than falling sharply. Mining investment grew by an average of about 0.5 per cent a quarter and private gross fixed capital formation by about 1.6 per cent a quarter over the same period. Mr Taylor's office cited a 2024 Minerals Council of Australia analysis, which the council's own material showed covered 2013 to 2023 and tracked a list of major projects rather than economy-wide investment.
context: Business investment growth has slowed since early 2024, and the Minerals Council has argued that the pipeline of major resources projects is weakening. The official data do not show a sharp decline in the level of investment under the current government.

findings: Mr Taylor's office said the figure summed net overseas migration for the five years from 2022-23 to 2026-27: two years of ABS actual figures and three years of budget forecasts, totalling 1.791 million. The two post-pandemic years, 2022-23 and 2023-24, account for 54 per cent of that total. Summing the forecasts for the next five years instead gives about 1.27 million, because net migration is forecast to fall sharply. Migration experts consulted by AAP FactCheck said the post-pandemic surge was driven largely by fewer departures, partly because of Coalition-era visa extensions, and that Labor's later delay in tightening student visa rules also contributed.
context: AAP FactCheck did not give the article a verdict label; it assessed the context of a figure used by several Coalition frontbenchers, including Opposition Leader Peter Dutton in his budget reply and Nationals leader David Littleproud on 4BC radio. The arithmetic behind the figure is correct for the period chosen; the dispute is over mixing past actual figures with future forecasts and over the causes of the surge.

findings: Budget Paper No. 4 for 2024-25, cited by Mr Taylor's office, projects a 36,008 increase in average staffing across the general government sector between 2021-22 and 2024-25. It gives no location breakdown and includes bodies outside the Australian Public Service such as the Australian Federal Police and ASIO. Australian Public Service Commission headcount data show a net rise of 26,153 APS employees between June 2022 and June 2024, of whom 7,464 were in Canberra and 18,689 (71.5 per cent) elsewhere, including more than 5,000 in Melbourne and 3,000 in Sydney. Even if the entire gap between the APS and budget figures were in Canberra, the maximum would be about 17,000.
context: The figure was used repeatedly by Coalition frontbenchers in early 2025, including by Mr Taylor on Channel 7's Sunrise on 8 January 2025 and in the Liberal Party's 'Priorities of a Dutton Coalition Government' document. The dispute is about location, not the overall growth in public-sector staffing, which the budget papers do project. Mr Taylor's office directed AAP FactCheck to the budget table but did not provide evidence that the roles were Canberra-based.

findings: ABS national accounts show income tax paid by individuals rose 27.3 per cent in nominal terms between the March quarter 2022 ($71.5 billion) and the September quarter 2023 ($91.0 billion). That period includes about two months of the previous Coalition government; from the June quarter 2022 the rise was 23.9 per cent. The rise was not a record: larger 18-month increases occurred in 1963-65 (43.5 per cent), 1969-70 (40.9 per cent), 1973-74 (107.2 per cent) and in the first 18 months of the Fraser government (41.7 per cent). Measured as a share of gross household income, income tax rose from 15.1 to 17.2 per cent, an increase of 13.6 per cent, which was also not a record.
context: A spokesman for Mr Taylor confirmed to RMIT ABC Fact Check that the figure compared the March 2022 and September 2023 quarterly ABS tax figures. Mr Taylor had used an 'over 27 per cent' figure in press releases on 6 and 13 December 2023 and repeated it on ABC Insiders on 11 February 2024. The Parliamentary Budget Office's explainer on bracket creep describes how income tax collections rise with wages even without rate changes.

findings: OECD data for the year to March 2023 put Australia's core inflation (consumer prices excluding food and energy) at 6.6 per cent, above Germany (5.8 per cent), the United Kingdom, the United States and the euro area (5.6 per cent each), Canada (4.9 per cent), Italy (4.7 per cent), France (3.5 per cent) and Japan (2.4 per cent). The latest comparable figure for the EU27, for the December quarter 2022, was 4.7 per cent against Australia's 5.5 per cent. Australia's core inflation was nonetheless below the OECD average of 7.2 per cent.
context: Mr Taylor made the comparison several times in early May 2023, including in an Australian Financial Review opinion piece on 2 May and on ABC News Breakfast on 4 May. Australia is not a member of the G7; the comparison was with its members, using the OECD's internationally comparable measure.

findings: ABS overseas migration data show net overseas migration peaked at 555,800 in the year to September 2023, then fell to 364,820 a year later and to 305,570 in the year to June 2025. ANU demographer Alan Gamlen put the five-year average at about 260,000 a year. Gross arrivals were 568,370 in the year to June 2025, below the 607,870 recorded in the year to December 2019. The 'half a million' figure applied to one post-pandemic year, not to migration 'per year' at the time of the statement.
context: Experts consulted by AAP FactCheck said the 2022-23 spike was a post-pandemic rebound driven partly by Coalition-era visa settings, including fee waivers and pandemic visas that reduced departures, and by Labor's 2022 decision to lift the permanent intake. Senator Hume's office did not respond to AAP FactCheck's request for evidence. She repeated the figure on Sky News on 16 and 19 February 2026.

findings: Tax law academics and a Treasury spokesperson identified existing and historical taxes levied on unrealised value: state land taxes in Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania and South Australia; the Commonwealth land tax levied from 1910 to 1953; capital gains tax 'exit' rules that deem assets to be disposed of at market value when a taxpayer ceases to be an Australian resident; and accruals-based taxation of financial arrangements for superannuation funds with $100 million or more in assets.
context: The statement was made during debate over the proposed tax on superannuation balances above $3 million, which would include unrealised gains. AAP FactCheck's article addressed similar statements by Senators Andrew Bragg and Jane Hume; Senator Bragg argued his claim related to Commonwealth rather than state law. Senator Hume did not respond to a request for evidence.

findings: Services Australia figures show average processing times for age pension claims rose from 35 days in 2021-22 to 76 days in 2023-24, and low income health care card claims took 6.6 times longer in 2023-24 than in 2020-21. The latest data at the time of the statement showed waits had fallen to 32 days for the age pension and 16 days for the low income card in the December quarter of 2024, below the 52 and 48 days recorded in 2019-20. The figures Senator Hume cited were accurate for 2023-24 but out of date by March 2025.
context: Services Australia's average staffing fell to 28,519 in 2023-24 and was funded to rise to 30,218 in 2024-25 following the 2023-24 MYEFO and the 2024-25 budget. ANU's Peter Whiteford told AAP FactCheck that using pandemic years as a baseline 'can be misleading'. Senator Hume's office did not respond to AAP FactCheck's request for evidence. She gave similar figures on Sky News in early April 2025.

findings: Senator Hume's office said the figure compares total payments forecast in the 2022 Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Outlook with those in the 2024-25 Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook for 2023-24 to 2027-28. Economists consulted by AAP FactCheck said that comparison mixes deliberate policy decisions with 'parameter' changes such as inflation and population growth: the 2022 PEFO assumed inflation would peak at 4.25 per cent when it was already 6.1 per cent at the election. UNSW accounting academic David Bond's reconciliation of the budget papers attributed $111 billion (about 40 per cent) of the rise in payments from 2023-24 to 2026-27 to Labor policy decisions and $117 billion to parameter variations; economist Chris Richardson put net policy spending at $124 billion.
context: AAP FactCheck did not give the article a one-word verdict; it found the figure 'problematic' and also found that Labor's counter-claim that Peter Dutton would cut $347 billion mischaracterised his comments. Opposition Leader Peter Dutton used the same figure on ABC Insiders in February 2025. The exact date of Senator Hume's Instagram post is not stated in the fact-check.

findings: NAB's 17 August 2026 newsletter described a hypothetical scenario in which rents would need to rise 25 to 30 per cent if rental yields rose by one percentage point and prices stayed flat; it did not forecast that rents would rise by 30 per cent, and NAB said in a note on 18 August that the figure 'was not a forecast'. Ray White, which Senator Hume cited as 'doubling down', told AAP FactCheck that its 30 per cent figure 'was not a forecast of rent growth' but a scenario with unchanged prices that it considered unlikely.
context: AAP FactCheck's verdict was given on Angus Taylor's statement in Question Time the previous day; the article records that Senator Hume 'made a similar claim'. The two statements are recorded separately on PUBLIC RECORD.

findings: The government's Constitutional Expert Group advised the Referendum Working Group that the Voice 'does not confer rights, much less special rights', and would not change or remove any right of other Australians. Public law and discrimination law academics consulted by AAP FactCheck (Gabrielle Appleby, Jennifer Nielsen and Alice Taylor) said the proposed body would create at most a right to be heard, that it was based on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples' status as First Peoples rather than race, and that it was consistent with the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 and with the international conventions Australia has ratified.
context: The statement was made in May 2023 during the campaign on the Voice referendum. The legal effect of the proposed amendment was contested throughout the campaign; AAP FactCheck's assessment relied on the Constitutional Expert Group's advice and on academic legal opinion. Senator Cash's office declined to comment when asked for evidence. The referendum was defeated on 14 October 2023.

findings: Defence officials told Senate estimates on 26 February 2025 that the People's Liberation Army Navy's live-fire drills of 21 and 22 February 2025 took place in international waters in the Tasman Sea. Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, a state's territorial sea extends 12 nautical miles from its coast and its exclusive economic zone to 200 nautical miles; the high seas lie beyond. International law experts consulted by AAP FactCheck said the drills were not in Australian waters and that live-fire exercises in Australia's territorial sea would have breached the convention.
context: Senator Paterson's office told AAP FactCheck he had 'misspoken' and meant to say 'in our region', pointing to other occasions on which he had used that phrase. The same fact-check addressed statements by Andrew Hastie and David Coleman. The drills caused commercial aircraft to divert after a broadcast warning, which was not disputed.

findings: Defence officials told Senate estimates on 26 February 2025 that China's live-fire drills of 21 and 22 February 2025 took place in international waters in the Tasman Sea; the government said at the time they occurred on the 'high seas'. Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, a state's territorial sea extends 12 nautical miles from its coast and its exclusive economic zone to 200 nautical miles. ANU international law professor Donald Rothwell said 'There was never any debate that the PLAN live-fire incident took place in the high seas' and that the drill's location had been conflated with the later circumnavigation through Australia's exclusive economic zone. Deakin University's Claudio Bozzi noted that live-fire exercises are permitted in international waters and that prior notification is protocol rather than a legal requirement.
context: Asked about the claim, Mr Hastie told AAP FactCheck the PLA Navy had 'irresponsibly' conducted live-fire exercises during an 'unprecedented' circumnavigation of Australia, causing 49 aircraft to divert without notice; he did not withdraw the 'our waters' wording. James Paterson and David Coleman made similar statements in February 2025, which AAP FactCheck addressed in the same article.

findings: The 2024 National Defence Strategy added $50.3 billion over the decade to 2033-34 compared with the funding trajectory in the Coalition's 2020 Defence Strategic Update. The 2024 Integrated Investment Program reprioritised $72.8 billion over the decade ($22.5 billion over four years), but Defence told Senate estimates that most of that was unapproved spending: of more than 540 projects, 188 were closed or merged, 45 delayed, 16 reduced in scope and 32 added or accelerated, with the 'vast majority' of approved projects unaffected. Defence analysts consulted by AAP FactCheck said the money was moved within the Defence budget, largely to AUKUS submarines and frigates, rather than removed from it. The 2023 Defence Strategic Review had found that $42 billion of Coalition-era announcements had never been provisioned in the budget.
context: AAP FactCheck rated Mr Dutton's statement that Labor had 'cut' or 'ripped' $80 billion out of Defence false. PUBLIC RECORD classifies Mr Hastie's 'cuts and delays' wording as mixed: the reprioritisation of $72.8 billion included project delays, cancellations and reductions in scope, while overall Defence funding increased over the decade. At a joint doorstop in Belmont, Western Australia, Mr Hastie pointed to scaled-back projects including F-35 aircraft, infantry fighting vehicles and two supply ships. Neither Mr Dutton nor Mr Hastie responded to AAP FactCheck's request for evidence.

findings: The CSIRO's GenCost 2024-25 final report gives a 2024 levelised cost range of $111 to $178 per megawatt hour for black coal and $120 to $168 for solar and wind with firming, with near-identical midpoints ($144.50 and $144). For 2030 the ranges are $103 to $174 for coal (midpoint $138.50) and $76 to $116 for firmed renewables (midpoint $96). The post used only the low end of the 2024 coal range and omitted the 2030 part of the chart. GenCost's lead author and a CSIRO spokesperson told AAP FactCheck that midpoints are the reasonable comparison and that renewables remain the lowest-cost new-build generation technology.
context: The lowest point of the 2024 coal cost range is below the lowest point of the firmed-renewables range, which is the basis of the post. Senator Canavan's office pointed AAP FactCheck to his opinion piece in Central Queensland Today, which he had also posted on Facebook. AAP FactCheck's verdict was that the claim misleads by relying on one end of one year's range.

findings: Four AEMO market notices were issued on the day Liddell's final unit was powered down, as the post showed; three were subsequently cancelled. AEMO's own explainer says a 'lack of reserve level 1' forecast 'simply provides an indication to the market to encourage more generation' and has 'no impact to power system security or reliability'. AEMO's quarterly reports show such notices are routine: 19 in the March 2023 quarter, 45 in the December 2022 quarter and 89 in the September 2022 quarter. Energy analysts Alison Reeve (Grattan Institute) and Bruce Mountain (Victoria University) said neither the New South Wales notices nor a South Australian intervention notice could be attributed to Liddell's closure.
context: The notices were real, but the fact-check found no evidence linking them to the closure of Liddell, and the type of notice involved is a routine market signal rather than a warning of supply failure. PUBLIC RECORD classifies the claim as mixed because the notices existed as described while the implied connection to the closure was not supported. No response from Senator Canavan is recorded in the fact-check.

findings: Economists Paul Burke (ANU) and John Quiggin (University of Queensland) and tax law professor Michael Dirkis (University of Sydney) told RMIT ABC Fact Check that the New Vehicle Efficiency Standard is not a tax because it raises no government revenue: it sets fleet-wide emissions limits on manufacturers, with tradeable credits and penalties for non-compliance. The Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries, whose modelling was cited for specific price rises, said its modelling of penalties and credits 'is not a forecast on price impacts'. The fact-check concluded that 'the government's proposal does not amount to a new tax' and that claims of specific price rises were not supported by the industry modelling cited.
context: The fact-check's headline subject was Opposition Leader Peter Dutton; the McKenzie and O'Brien release was cited as one example of the same claim, alongside statements by Angus Taylor and Michaelia Cash. PUBLIC RECORD classifies the claim as mixed: the 'tax' characterisation was found not to apply, and the price-impact figure was not supported by the modelling cited, while the policy does impose penalties on manufacturers that could affect prices. No response from Senator McKenzie is recorded in the fact-check.

findings: Mr Littleproud's and Angus Taylor's offices said the figure summed ABS net overseas migration for 2022-23 and 2023-24 with budget forecasts for 2024-25 to 2026-27, giving 1.791 million; 54 per cent of that total comes from the two post-pandemic years already past. Summing the forecasts for the next five years, as the wording 'over the next five years' implies, gives about 1.27 million, because net migration is forecast to fall sharply from 2024-25. Migration experts Anna Boucher, Alan Gamlen and Abul Rizvi told AAP FactCheck that the post-pandemic surge largely reflected reduced departures and the policies of both Coalition and Labor governments, and that net migration should not be equated with arrivals.
context: The same figure was used by Angus Taylor and Peter Dutton in March 2025 and is recorded separately for Mr Taylor. The 1.8 million figure is the sum for a five-year period that includes two years already elapsed; applied to the next five years, as stated, it is overstated by about half a million.

findings: The offices of Mr Littleproud and Michael Sukkar said the figure came from Master Builders Australia and supplied a table comparing ABS average values of new home building approvals in Greater Sydney between the December quarters of 2022 and 2023. That comparison measured overall cost increases from labour, materials and regulation, not the cost of the 2022 National Construction Code seven-star change, as Master Builders itself confirmed. Other estimates of the code change were $2,972 to $5,905 (Australian Glass and Window Association), $20,000 to $30,000 (Master Builders Queensland), $25,000 (Housing Industry Association) and $464 to $7,830 in capital costs with $630 to $9,693 in energy-bill savings (ACIL Allen regulatory impact statement). Building researchers Trivess Moore (RMIT) and Michael Ambrose (CSIRO) said no rigorous study supported $60,000.
context: The same claim was made by Peter Dutton in October 2024 and by Michael Sukkar on 2CC radio. Industry estimates of the code change vary widely, but none located by AAP FactCheck approached $60,000. Mr Littleproud's office did not issue a correction.

findings: Mr Littleproud's office said the figures came from Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries modelling from February 2024, which used a stricter draft of the policy, 2023 sales data, the Ford Ranger as a proxy for the Everest, and petrol-only RAV4 models that Toyota stopped selling in June 2024; the chamber itself described the figures as 'outdated somewhat'. Applying the legislated formula, AAP FactCheck calculated that every 2025 RAV4 model would earn a credit of $3,390 to $3,880 (confirmed by Toyota), that the highest-emitting Everest would incur a penalty of $3,210 (an average of $420 across nine models), and that by 2029 RAV4 penalties would be $4,420 to $4,910 rather than $11,000. The Ford Everest was not Australia's most popular vehicle in 2024. Transport researchers Robin Smit (UTS) and Hussein Dia (Swinburne) said fleet-wide penalties do not translate into fixed price rises for particular models.
context: The New Vehicle Efficiency Standard came into effect on 1 January 2025, the day of the interview. A spokesperson for Mr Littleproud confirmed the Ford Ranger figures were used for the Everest and provided more detailed chamber projections. AAP FactCheck later found a social-media version of the same figures false and noted that Peter Dutton repeated the claim.

findings: Using Australian Taxation Office excise rates ($43.22 per litre of pure alcohol for keg beer above 3.5 per cent, with the first 1.15 per cent exempt), AAP FactCheck calculated that a 50-litre keg of 4.6 per cent beer attracts $74.55 in excise, or 42 cents per 285-millilitre pot. With 64 cents of GST on a $7 pot, total tax is about $1.06, or about 15 per cent of the price. An 8 per cent beer would be taxed at about 21 per cent; packaged beer is taxed at a higher rate ($61.32 per litre of alcohol), reaching about 40 per cent of the price of a $60 slab. Brewers Association figures of about 60 cents of tax per pot broadly matched.
context: Mr Littleproud was arguing for a pause in the twice-yearly indexation of alcohol excise for beer served in pubs. Beer excise is indexed to inflation every six months, as he said; the fact-check found the share of a pot's price made up of tax to be well under half. Mr Littleproud's office did not respond when AAP FactCheck asked for the basis of the figure.

findings: Landholders who host new transmission lines receive compensation for easements and, in several states, additional annual payments: New South Wales and Victoria pay about $200,000 per kilometre of line hosted over 20 to 25 years, and Queensland about $300,000 per kilometre. AAP FactCheck also cited the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water and the Australian Energy Infrastructure Commissioner on easement compensation. The statement that transmission-line hosts receive no financial benefit was not correct.
context: Asked for evidence, Mr Littleproud's office said he had misspoken. In a statement to AAP FactCheck he said: 'I acknowledge I misspoke in my answer in that interview. What I was trying to articulate was that those forced into hosting transmission lines don't receive an equitable level of financial benefit in comparison to the wind and solar hosts.' AAP FactCheck noted he had not otherwise publicly corrected the statement. AAP FactCheck's 'Mostly False' rating is recorded here as contradicted because the literal statement was shown to be incorrect; the clarified claim about the relative size of payments is a different claim that the fact-check did not assess.

findings: ABS national accounts to the September quarter 2024 recorded seven consecutive quarterly falls in GDP per capita, the longest run in the series that begins in 1973, with a cumulative fall of about 2.1 per cent since December 2022. Measured by depth, larger per-capita falls occurred in the June quarter 2020 (6.9 per cent), in 1981–83 (6.2 per cent) and in 1990–91 (3 per cent), and economic historians cited falls of around 20 per cent in 1929–31 and 17 per cent in the 1890s. The claim holds for the number of consecutive quarters but not for the size of the fall.
context: 'Worst' can be measured by duration or by depth. Senator Hanson's spokesperson told AAP FactCheck she was referring to the number of consecutive quarters of negative per-capita growth. AAP FactCheck rated the claim 'mostly false'; PUBLIC RECORD classifies it as mixed because it is accurate on one measure and inaccurate on the other.

findings: ABS net overseas migration data to September 2025 gave 1.23 million net migrants over the preceding three years, an average of about 1,122 a day. The 1,375 figure corresponds to total population growth per day in an analysis published by The Australian, which includes natural increase (births minus deaths); that analysis put daily net migration at 1,091. Later ABS data to December 2025 put the three-year average at about 1,060 a day.
context: Population growth and net overseas migration are different measures. The same figure appeared in a 2GB interview on 16 June 2026 and in a One Nation Instagram graphic on 9 June 2026 that itself distinguished the 1,375 population figure from 1,091 for net migration.

findings: Section 17 of South Australia's Local Government (Elections) Act 1999 requires council candidates to be Australian citizens enrolled to vote, and a provision that had allowed certain non-citizen former councillors to stand was removed in 2021. Non-citizen residents and ratepayers could previously enrol to vote in council elections, but an amendment effective 1 January 2026 restricted voting to citizens and a legacy group of British subjects enrolled before 26 January 1984. The SA Electoral Commissioner confirmed this to AAP FactCheck.
context: Two by-elections called before the 1 January 2026 change were held in February 2026 under the old voting rules. Senator Hanson's office referred AAP FactCheck to an Electoral Commission of South Australia page for the 2022 elections describing non-citizen enrolment to vote; that page did not say non-citizens could stand as candidates.

findings: The figures come from three datasets that do not measure the same thing. ABS data record about 737,000 overseas arrivals in 2022–23, including returning Australians, of whom 83,700 held skilled visas. The 51,605 figure is the number of temporary skilled visas granted to primary applicants that year, not arrivals, and a further 68,922 permanent skilled visas were granted. The Department of Home Affairs told AAP FactCheck that 10,589 temporary and permanent visas were granted to construction-industry occupations in 2022–23; the 1,800 figure is close to the 1,626 permanent and 1,967 temporary visas granted on a narrower list of core construction trades.
context: Whether 'construction industry' means all construction occupations or a short list of trades changes the figure by a factor of about six. Similar comments were made in an SBS interview in May 2026 and a News24 interview on 6 August 2026.

findings: The ABS 2021 Census estimated 122,494 people were homeless on census night, a figure close to the one used. Of those, 7,636 (6 per cent) were in the 'improvised dwellings, tents or sleeping out' category the ABS treats as sleeping rough; the largest group, 47,895 (39 per cent), were living in severely crowded dwellings. The number is approximately right for homelessness under the ABS definition and about 17 times the ABS figure for people sleeping rough.
context: The ABS definition of homelessness is broader than 'rooflessness' and includes severely crowded dwellings, supported accommodation, boarding houses and staying temporarily with other households.

findings: ATO taxation statistics for 2022–23 record 216,942 people under 35 reporting a net capital gain, compared with 286,870 aged 35 to 49 and 717,658 aged over 35 in total; the largest five-year age bracket was 35 to 39. In 2023–24, 18 to 34-year-olds reported $1.94 billion in net capital gains against $9.78 billion for 35 to 49-year-olds, and 5.2 per cent of 18 to 34-year-old tax filers reported a gain compared with 15.4 per cent of those over 65.
context: The figures in the speech match an article in The Australian that described under-35s as the largest growth cohort over ten years, not the largest cohort. Economist Saul Eslake told AAP FactCheck older age groups would be most affected by the proposed changes.

findings: The National Greenhouse Gas Inventory quarterly update to September 2023 attributes 17.9 per cent of Australia's emissions to agriculture, while the land use, land-use change and forestry sector offset 13.9 per cent of total emissions. Scientists from the CSIRO and the Global Carbon Project told AAP FactCheck that no single sector can count natural sinks as cancelling its own emissions.
context: Atmospheric methane is more than 260 per cent above pre-industrial levels and the UN Environment Programme attributes about a quarter of current warming to it.

findings: The ABS told AAP FactCheck that its estimated resident population, which underlies the population clock that passed 27 million on 24 January 2024, counts anyone in Australia for 12 of 16 months regardless of visa type. Most of the 2.76 million temporary visa holders recorded by the Department of Home Affairs at 31 December 2023, including 701,868 New Zealanders on Special Category visas and 547,075 student visa holders, are therefore already included; only the 601,051 visitor-visa holders would mostly be excluded.
context: The ABS 12/16-month rule determines residency for population estimates independently of visa status.

findings: Australian Institute of Marine Science records show mass bleaching on the reef was first documented with full-scale surveys in 1998, followed by 2002, 2016, 2017, 2020 and 2022, with the 2024 event the fifth in eight years. A University of Queensland coral scientist told AAP FactCheck that cores from corals hundreds of years old show no earlier mass bleaching events, and a co-author of the University of Sydney study cited in the speech said it examined reef growth over 20,000 to 30,000-year cycles and did not look at bleaching.
context: The speech cited a University of Sydney study on reef growth cycles; its co-author told AAP FactCheck the study did not support the claim.

findings: Using ABS 2020–21 value-of-production data for the 48 statistical areas wholly or partly within Farrer, an analysis by Flinders University water economist Professor Sarah Wheeler for AAP FactCheck estimated the electorate's agricultural output at about $4.4 billion of a $71 billion national total, around 6 per cent. The 40 per cent figure matches the whole Murray-Darling Basin, which the Murray-Darling Basin Authority says produces around 40 per cent of Australia's agricultural output and which is roughly eight times the size of the electorate.
context: In a Facebook video on 28 June 2026 Mr Farley applied the 40 per cent figure to the Southern Murray-Darling Basin, an area about four times larger than Farrer.
